Keeping Your Heating and Cooling System Running Well

A heating and cooling system that gets regular care uses less energy, lasts longer and keeps the house more comfortable. Most homes rely on a heat pump, a furnace, a central air conditioner, or a heat pump paired with a furnace for backup heat. Whatever the equipment, the same handful of maintenance tasks keeps it healthy.

Change the air filter
The air filter is the most important supply in the system. A clogged filter starves the blower of air, makes the heat pump work harder and lets dust settle on the indoor coil. Check the filter every month during heavy heating and cooling seasons, and do a filter change at least every three months. Pleated filters with a MERV rating of 8 to 11 trap fine dust without restricting airflow too much.

Schedule a yearly tune-up
Have a licensed HVAC contractor perform a tune-up once a year: in spring for the cooling system and in fall for the heating system. A heat pump does both jobs, so it benefits from a check before each season. During the tune-up the contractor should:
- tighten electrical connections and measure the voltage and current on the compressor and the blower motor, since loose connections and high current draw shorten motor life;
- check the refrigerant charge, because a heat pump that is low on refrigerant heats and cools poorly;
- clean the indoor coil and the outdoor coil;
- lubricate moving parts such as the blower motor bearings;
- inspect the condensate drain and flush it if it is slow, since a blocked drain can flood the air handler and raise indoor humidity;
- test the system controls to make sure the starting cycle and shut-off sequence run correctly.

Look after the outdoor unit
The outdoor unit holds the compressor and the outdoor coil. Keep at least two feet of clear space around it, rake away leaves and grass clippings, and never stack firewood against the cabinet. After a snowstorm, brush snow off the top and sides so the heat pump can defrost properly.

Use the thermostat well
A programmable thermostat saves energy by lowering the setpoint while you sleep or are away. In winter, a setpoint of 68°F while you are home is a good starting point. With a heat pump, avoid deep setbacks, which can switch on the backup electric heat.

Watch indoor humidity
In summer, the central air conditioner or heat pump removes moisture as it cools. Keep indoor humidity between 30 and 50 percent; if it stays higher, ask the contractor whether the system is oversized or the airflow is set too high.

Seal and insulate the ductwork
Leaky ductwork in an attic or crawl space can waste a fifth of the air the blower moves. Seal joints with mastic or foil tape, not cloth duct tape, and insulate ducts that run through unconditioned space.
